units.text: Original Articles. THE PE VALENCE IN INDIA OF GASTRIC AND DUODENAL ULCER AND ALLIED CONDITIONS OF THE UPPER ABDOMEN WITH SOME OBSERVATIONS ON THE DIAGNOSIS AND TREATMENT

The diagnosis of chronic abdominal diseases is, in the case of many Indian village patients, beset with difficulties not obtaining in Western countries. This is due to the prevailing high percentage of illiteracy and the consequent lack of power of observation on the part of ignorant patients, making history-taking at times very unsatisfactory. This condition of things is intensified to a certain extent by the unavailability of up-to-date methods of diagnosis. This is most obvious in the rural districts remote from the large cities.
It is gratifying, however, to note a vast improvement in this respect in recent years.

In this country the inability to secure accurate and trustworthy data in recording the patient's history often tests severely the diagnostic acumen of the examining physician in making an accurate diagnosis.

The surgical treatment of abdominal disease in India is conducted with the further handicap of lower resistance of Indian patients to surgical procedure, as compared with those of the Anglo-Saxon races. An exception to this may be found among the sturdier races inhabiting the colder climates of the Northern and Frontier Provinces.

An illustration of this contention is the fact that there was but one surgical death in two hundred and eighty major operations upon Europeans?European or American extraction?in the Miraj Hospital during the past 20 years. This death from postoperative pneumonia occurred in a case of extensively infiltrated, infected cancer of the neck which had been long neglected. Prominent among the chronic conditions of the upper abdomen prevailing in India is gastric and duodenal ulcer, a disease which fifteen years ago was not thought to be particularly prevalent in India. In 1908, in an attempt to ascertain the incidence of gastric ulcer, the writer found that in the previous year no case of gastric ulcer had been reported in four large Presidency Hospitals. Similar evidence was obtained from several rural districts.
Government medical reports tabulated very few cases.

Between 1901 to the end of 1908, the writer operated on 70 cases of gastric and duodenal ulcer, which were reported at the Bombay Medical Congress in 1909. The first case, a duodenal ulcer, was operated in 1901. An anterior gastroenterostomy was done, employing a Murphy button. The button receded into the stomach and was removed four months later by gastrotomy on account of the gastric distress which it occasioned. At the second operation the stoma was found patent. This patient is still alive and in good health.
In the discussion which followed the report of these seventy cases, the opinion was expressed by some that they did not consider the prevalence of ulcer widespread in this country.

Up to the end of 1919, five hundred and ninety-one cases of gastric and duodenal ulcer were operated upon in the Miraj Hospital; 75 of these patients were operated on in 1919. These patients have come from various parts of Western India, chiefly from the rural districts. These facts, together with the now frequent performance of gast ro-enterostomy reported from almost every part of India, are sufficient to establish the fact of a widespread incidence of gastric and duodenal ulcer in India.
The extensive prevalence of cancer of the stomach, which develops frequently upon chronic ulcer, is further proof of the above contention, were such proof needed.

In our earlier experience, we assumed that ulcer was a condition prevailing in those districts in which " jwari " and the heavier grains formed the principal articles of diet and where rice is eaten sparingly. In the light of the more recent experience of practitioners located in the rice-consuming areas, we have had to modify our former impressions. The irritating causative agent in the development of ulcer is, after all, not the character of the food itself, but much more likely the excessive stimulation produced by the ingestion of hot curries taken in conjunction with poorly cooked and inadequately masticated food.

The average dirty septic mouth so commonly observed in India must be regarded as an everpresent source of. potential focal infection provocative of gastric ulcer and other intestinal disorders. The presence of lime in the mouth of the beetle-nut chewer may exert an antiseptic influence in these septic mouths which inhibit bacterial growth, albeit the , lime is itself an exciting factor in the development of buccal cancer, [Dec., 1920. Alcohol, once (thought to be a factor in the etiology of gastric ulcer, cannot be so regarded in the case of Indians, comparatively few of whom, i'lii the villages at least, are addicted to its excessive use.
In a perusal of our casehistories this statement is confirmed.

Chronic persistent dyspepsia so called, or gastritis per sc without the presence of an ulcer, or the existence of some allied affection of the gall bladder or vermiform appendix, is a comparatively rare affection. Chronic dyspepsia is, however, a frequent precursor of gastric and duodenal ulcer and, when attended with pain, may connote the actual presence of an ulcer.
A well-developed case of ulcer is comparatively easy of diagnosis. Early cases, and these exhibiting an ill-defined history, are often difficult of determination.
Some of the signs of gastric and duodenal ulcer may be considered, as illustrated in our Miraj experience:?
Age.?The disease is most common between 25th and 45th years.
Symptoms: Hcematemesis and melcena.?

In approximately 65 per cent, of the cases treated in the Miraj Hospital, no history of bleeding from the stomach or bowel was obtainable. The comparative infrequence of this symptom as compared with the writings of some clinicians is probably due, in part at least, to ignorance and lack of observation on the part of .these patients.

In the examination of the gastric contents and stools occult blood will more often be observed. In our experience, the finding of occult blood in the vomitus or stools is not essential to the diagnosis of ulcer, though confirmatory.

Vomiting.?Involuntary vomiting is another symptom not uncommonly absent, though in most of our patients we have observed the habit of voluntarily emptying the stomach as a means of relief from gastric distress?a very suggestive sign of ulcer.
Fulness and heaviness in the epigastrium is invariably complained of for some hours after meals?a symptom, equally, if not more, common in gastric cancer.

Visible peristalsis may be observed in many cases, and, if accompanied by pain, is helpfully diagnostic. In late cases .the peristalsis is best noted at night after a heavy evening meal. Visible peristalsis is indicative of pyloric stenosis, and may also be present in duodenal ulcer without stricture. Nausea, in our experience, is not a constant symptom. It should be remembered, however, that the average Indian patient vomits less readily under ordinary circumstances than the European. His stomach is less sensitive to nauseating reflexes.

Loss of appetite increases pari passu with the progress of the disease. These patients, however, complain more of being compelled to decline food from the sheer dread of pain rather than the actual loss of appetite?another positively suggestive sign of ulcer.

Acidity.?A sour stomach is quite as indicative of gastric neurosis as of ulcer, though this symptom is frequently present in ulcer. Water brush vomiting is more common in ulcer. We have generally found acidity higher in duodenal ithan in gastric ulcer.
Food relief is indicative of duodenal ulcer, but may be present in gastric neuroses.

Pain.?Moynihan places the greatest reliance upon this symptom, as do also the Mayos and others of large experience in gastric surgery. Without pain, the existence of a gastric or duodenal ulcer should 'be questioned. In its absence an operation should be considered inadvisable. Haemorrhage, which may be painless, might be considered an exception to this rule. The character of the pain is sufficiently described in the books and needs no special description here, except to say that the pain immediately after meals is indicative of gastric, and two to four hours after meals of duodenal, ulcer.

The reference of the pain to the back or lower dorsal region is frequently noted in duodenal ulcer, and is generally due to the adhesion" of the ulcer to the pancreas. Disturbance of sleep by the pain is commonly complained of.
Tenderness.?In practically all cases of pyloric and duodenal ulcer there is a tender point corresponding to the ulcer area.
Constipation is invariable and often very obstinate. Emaciation is often so excessive in the cases we see in India as to suggest malignancy. It is, however, much slower in development than in cancer.

Anaemia obtains in late cases, is not usually well marked, but may be a prominent feature where haemorrhage has occurred. Blood examination.?The blood picture may ?be that of secondary anaemia, or may show a moderate leucocytosis. Gastric contents.?Examination of the gastric contents, while not essential to diagnosis, is of corroborative value and should always be employed. Superacidity and supersecretion may both be present, the former most commonly, and its presence excludes cancer with few exceptions. Hyperacidity is not a necessary sign of gastric ulcer. We have not infrequently confirmed the diagnosis of ulcer with normal or sub-acidity present. In one case we found a duodenal ulcer present at operation in which the gastric analysis showed absence of free H CI.
This condition was probably a late development in a long-standing case of ulcer, with gastric atrophy.

Roentgenography.?The employment of X-ray is of very great utility in the' corroborative diagnosis. Some surgeons now-a-days depend upon the X-ray findings almost to the exclusion of other tests. In most of the advanced cases we see in India, X-rays are not indispensable in making a diagnosis. We employ X-rays in doubtful and early cases, but with our present experience do not feel competent to correctly interpret the findings in every case and in our judgment .there are few X-ray specialists in India who can.

MdLure and Reynolds, of Boston, state that in certain cases Roentgen Ray findings are more confusing than helpful to diagnosis and that atypical X-ray findings may assist materially in making an incorrect diagnosis. Atropin should be used in conjunction with flouroscopy in order to eliminate spasm.

The employment of the stomach tube is still a simple, available and invaluable instrument of diagnosis and its use is seldom objected to by Indians. The Indian early morning custom of cleansing the throat by the introduction of the fingers, so familiar to us al'l, facilitates greatly the use of the stomach tube. In gastric disturbances assistants and students should be systematically taught to employ and intelligently interpret the findings connected with its use. No instrument is of greater utility in the palliative treatment of gastric disorders, not to mention its value in the treatment of bile tract disturbance, intestinal .obstruction and other intestinal conditions. It is our practice to flush out the stomach at the dlose of every gastric operation, and subsequently during the first forty-eight hours if there is distension, vomiting or evidence of a vicious circle. This, of course, must be done circumspectly with small quantities of water. In acute dilatation the stomach tube is indispensable. Its use is contra-indicated in suspected perforation of the stomach, but even here its employment soon after a full meal is not objectionable. Persistent vomiting due to anaesthesia is another indication for its use. I have here, referred to the use of the stomach tube somewhat irrelevantly, for the reason that few Indian assistants and practitioners are familiar with its proper use or utility, simple though it be.

Lastly, in the diagnosis of duodenal ulcer it should not be forgotten that in the early history of these cases the symptoms often occur in bouts lasting for days or weeks with similar intervals of comparative relief, the relief intervals becoming more infrequent, the gastric disturbance more persistent and the relation of pain to food intake more constant.
These " dyspeptic " attacks may obtain in gastric neuroses, but respond more promptly to rest and diet.

In India, in the long-standing cases of gastric and duodenal ulcer?the patients most commonly seeking surgical relief?the diagnosis is so obvious that " he who runs may read." The distinction between a gastric and duodenal ulcer is not always so apparent clinically?a distinction which is of no great practical value in a definitely operative case. We should also recognize the not infrequent experience of surgeons in cases with a fairly well-defined history and in which, on exposure of the stomach, a visible or palpable ulcer is not found. I have heard Dr. John Erdmen, a prominent New York surgeon, state, and claim confirmation by Dr. W. J. Mayo, that on several occasions he had opened the abdomen in anticipation of finding an ulcer when none was apparent, but later on with a recurrence of the symptoms a visible ulcer was demonstrated. These are evidently cases of duodenitis, or early nonindurated ulcer which in a later stage eventuates in a palpable induration.

Allied diseases.?The association of gall bladder and gall duct disease with that of the duodenum is well known. In India, especially among the rural population, oholeliathiasis is a frequent complaint as compared with Western countries. At least this had been our experience in Miraj. This comparatively lower incidence of gall bladder disease is apparently the happy result of Indian poverty in which over-eating is the exception and bodily exertion the rule.

It is our practice to examine the gall bladder and ducts in all cases of operation upon the upper abdomen, and in operations upon the lower abdomen where this is feasible and there is no contra-indication.
Gall bladder involvement was found only 25 times in 1,523 abdominal operations during the past five years.

In the majority of these cases patients came from the Presidency cities and larger towns. Civilization seems to have its drawbacks and gall bladder disease is one of them. The symptoms of gall bladder disease and cholecystitis have been so thoroughly described in the recent text-books that a restatement here would be superfluous. I desire simply to call attention here to the outstanding symptoms in the diagnosis, vis., no definite relation to meals, localization of the pain in the right sub-costa'l area often reflected to the region of the scapula, tenderness and rigidity in the gall bladder region, palpable gall bladder, flatulence, jaundice, colic and occasional fever.

In these rural districts of India, remembering always that India is mainly a nation of villages, the obese, flabby female, typical of gall stone disease, is conspicuous by her absence; withal it is a little surprising that cholecystitis is not more frequently observed in this country in view of the prevalence of gastric and duodenal ulcer and of other gastro-intestinal disorders of high incidence. Cholecystitis may, after all, be much more prevalent than we have been wont to suppose. This state of afifairs may be the result of the Indian's comparative insensibility to pain and his willingness to put up with it if it is not too prolonged or unbearable. The surgeon, in consequence, is deprived of facilities of observation and his impressions are possibly inconsistent with actual facts. Our own feeling is that, as opportunities for clinical investigation increase [Dec., 1920. pari passu with a larger experience in this field of surgery, we shall find, in common with our Western confreres, that cholecystitis is more prevalent in India than we have in the past been led to believe.

Appendix syndrome.?The well-known association of appendicitis with gall bladder and duodenal disease serves to help in the problem of diagnosis in doubtful cases of duodenal ulcer. Appendicitis is common enough in the cities and large towns of India. That it is less frequent among the village people, I think, is quite obvious; certainly to those of us whose patients come largely from the rural districts. We should like to say, however, that here again the incidence of appendicitis in the villages is greater than our earlier experience led us to suppose.

During the five-year period to December 31st, 1919, 354 appendices were removed in the Miraj Hospital. A large proportion of these were removed during the performance of other intraabdominal operations, practically all of which exhibited evidence of either a chronic appendicitis, or appendices that did not appear to be anatomically normal. During a period of 23 years, in a total of 3,320 abdominal operations there were 518 appendectomies, 164 of which were performed during the first eighteen years. These statistics are given in confirmation of our revised impressions as stated above.

I have not had time to consult our operation records with special reference to cases in which a provisional diagnosis of ulcer having been made and in which operation demonstrated the absence of an ulcer and the presence of chronic appendix as the only visible pathology. This circumstance, however, has not been infrequent. An appendix chronically inflamed or containing a concretion, or one adherent beneath a peritoneal membrane (retro-peritoneal), or buried behind the cfficum (retro-caeca!), is capable of producing the reflex pylorospasm symptomatically simulating gastric and duodenal ulcer. Such cases are common in the experience of modern surgeons. The diagnosis of an appendix syndrome is based on the inconstancy of the symptoms as compared with ulcer. Epigastric pain is the symptom most commonly complained of. but is less severe than ulcer pain and bears a fairly definite relation to meals. Food relief is absent as a rule. Acidity and a sour stomach are not infrequent. There is, however, little or no wasting and the food intake is not restricted. On palpation there is tenderness on the right iliac fossa wi'h more or less muscular rigidity. A history of previous attacks of pain in the right lower abdomen is suggestive. An X-ray examination may help to establish a diagnosis.
Operation on these patients may reveal a hypertrophied condition of the pyloric ring, the result of prolonged reflex spasm.
In several such cases we have performed pyloroplasty. In the light of further experience we now deem this unnecessary, a simple appendectomy being sufficient.

In a recent case, however, with ra:her marked pyloric hypertrophy, we did the Rammstedt operation now in vogue in the treatment of congenital hypertrophy of the pylorus. It is easy of performance and consists in splitting the pylorus longitudinally for an inch through serosa and musculosa, leaving the mucosa intact. A tag of adjacent omentum is stitched over the gap.

Cancer of the stomach.?During the five-year period to December 31, 1919, in a total of 298 operations upon the stomach and duodenum (270 of which were for the relief of ulcer), there were 21 cases of gastric cancer?1 in every 15 stomach operations. Patients considered inoperable were not, as a rule, admitted to hospital. All of these operated cases admitted only of palliative operation, viz., gastro-enterostomy.

The crux of the cancer problem is early diagnosis. None of the cases admitted during this five-year period were considered radically operable. In one operable case a gastrectomy was done in the present year with fatal result, from whatwas thought to be pulmonary embolism.

We have done but two other gastrectomies for cancer previous to the fiveyear period. The progress of cancer is rapid compared with Ulcer. Few of these patients realize the seriousness of their malady until they are beyond surgical relief. Medical practitioners are frequently guilty of similar tardiness.

The encouraging results of early radical operation for cancer of the stomach in Western countries should stimulate us to a more active propaganda and earlier intervention in such cases, though in India the task at present is not very hopeful.

Cancer developing upon, a pre-existing ulcer may give a long history of dyspepsia, which is apt to be misleading. The diagnosis of cancer can and should be made before the growth becomes palpable?-a stage which connotes inoperabili'.y, and spells early demise. The absence or insignificance of the pain in some cases of gastric cancer is also misleading. In the recent case of a nurse, pain was absent almost to the day of death. There was no palpable tumour.

Emaciation and occasional vomiting led to a gastric analysis which showed absent of free H CI and occult blood present. Exploration revealed an inoperable cancer of the lesser curvature with metastasis in the pelvis. Anorexia, loss of appetite, fulness and more or less constant dull pain in tne epigastrium with loss of weight, should lead to immediate further investigation, viz., the employment of gastric analysis and radiography. The vomiting of blood, sometimes painlessly, is more common than in ulcer. The finding of bits of tissue in the vomitus or on lavage is diagnostic of canter rather than ulcer. The presence of Boas Oppler Bacillus and the formation of lactic acid are not necessary to a positive diagnosis.

The absence of free H CI is the most significant thing in the analysis. The complete absence of free H CI is not, however, essential to a diagnosis, though it is invariably low, if not entirely absent. It has been the experience of surgeons, our own in one instance, to have a mass in the pyloric area, supposedly cancer, disappear after performance ofgastroenterostomy as demonstrated at a second abdominal section preparatory to excision.

Dilatation of fhe stomach and gastroptosis.? Stomachs, like noses, differ greatly in size and outline within normal physiological limits. The stomach or organic stenosis, and of long-standing cases of doudenal ulcer is large and the wall thickened, the lower border seldom reaches below the umbilicus. The dilated and ptosed stomach generally extends below this point and even into the false pelvis, such stomachs we have noted in pelvic operations apparently without causing symptoms. The habit of Indian women of binding the sari tightly above the body of the stomach may induce dilatation, and frequently produces gastroptosis. Only occasionally do these patients seek surgical relief. The city patient with a dilated stomach is usually neurotic. The chief complaint is gastric distension, discomfort rather than actual pain, and occasional vomiting; sleeplessness is a common symptom.

The diagnosis which is usually apparent may require the employment of air distension or X-rays for elucidation. In cases giving rise to symptoms, the use of the stomach tube, the application of a suitable abdominal belt, the correction of dress, and diet-measures appropriate for the city patient are neither available nor practical for the poor villager. Such patients should be given the help which surgery affords. We have performed gastroplication with shortening of the gastric hepatic ligament in three cases with satisfactory immediate result, but were unable to follow the patients to ascertain end results. Fixing the prolapsed stomach to the parietal peritoneum, we consider surgically unsound.
Coloptosis and gastroptosis are generally associated with sagging of the colon and prolapse and dilatation of caecum.

For this last condition we have several times plicated the caecum and colon; and, in a case recently, corrected the ptosis by anchoring the outer leaf of the ascending colonic mesentery laterally to the abdominal wall and extending'the anchorage well up under the liver, the sutures plicating the outer half of the mesocolon at the same time. The free border of the liver was anchored to the abdominal wall under the costal arch.
Gastric neuroses, such as nervous eructations, nervous vomiting, gastralgia, pylorospasm and achylia gastrica, are medical conditions which at times may call for differentiation.
Pylorospasm. in neuroses is frequently due to hyper-acidity or hyper-secretion, or the result of a reflex neuroses. The condition may simulate duodenal ulcer.

Chronic appendicitis (to which reference has already been made) is" the causative agent in some cases. For exploration in these cases the right rectus incision, two to three inches in length with the mid point an inch above the umbilicus, is the most suitable incision and can be extended up towards the stomach or down towards the caecum as desired.
Achylia gaslrica.?We have had several such cases.

The condition may be mistaken for ulcer if a gastric analysis is not made. Free H CI is absent and there may be a total absence of the gastric secretion. Fermentation and stagnation of food may result if motility is not good. In two such cases with stagnation of food, we performed a posterior gastroenterostomy, making a large stoma. There was immediate symptomatic relief in both patients. One we have been unable to follow. The other after three years has a partial recurrence of the symptoms.

Perforated gastric and duodenal ulcer.?In operations for ulcers we have on a number of occasions encountered evidence of a previously perforated and spontaneously healed ulcer. These patients showed a healthy gall bladder and appendix, but adhesions in the vicinity of the ulcer or between the mesocolon and the stomach at a distance from the site of the ulcer, and isolated enlarged glands in the colonic mesentery. Adhesions between the mesocolon and stomach may, however, result from gastritis accompanying non-perforated ulcer of the stomach.

The perforation in these cases must have been small and closed promptly by nature. On postoperative inquiry we ascertained a previous history of an attack of acute abdominal pain and distension months or years previously and lasting for several days, the attack meanwhile having been forgotten by the patient. I have no way of positively proving that a perforated ulcer may heal spontaneously, but the inference in these cases is in favour of this contention. I cite these instances not with the object of deferring immediate operation in cases of suspected perforation, but simply as a statement of a possible fact. We do knozu that a perforated ulcer may heal after simple drainage without closure of the perforation, since such cases have been reported. We have operated upon but one case of perforated ulcer in the past five years, due to the fact that cases of perforated ulcer occur in the village patients for whom surgical relief-is not obtainable.

Adhesions in the vicinity of the pylorus and first portion of the duodenum may give rise to symptoms simulating ulcer. The adhesions may result from a former cholecystitis, perforated and healed gastric or duodenal ulcer (assuming the foregoing contention to be true) or ulcerative colitis. In two instances we have found a cordlike band obstructing the outlet of the stomach in one and constricting the duodenum in [Dec., 1920. another.

On several occasions we have adhesions between the pylorus duodenum and the under surface of the liver, dragging the pylorus upward and preventing the proper emptying of the stomach. When the adhesions are extensive, gastro-enterostomy may be indicated. In a recent case clinically presenting all the characters of a duodenal ulcer as shown by X-rays and the presence of hsematemesis and melasna, the first portion of the duodenum and pylorus were so buried in adhesions that these structures were not visible. The adhesions in this case were evidently due to a duodenal ulcer, which was palpably present. A gastro-enterostomy was performed and the adhesions left undisturbed with gratifying result. In cases of adhesions without evidence of ulcers and where the adhesions appear to be the cause of the symptoms, simple division and peritonealization of the raw area should be performed. It is advisable always to remove the appendix at the same time, and the gall bladder also if indurated. In regard to abdominal adhesions in general, it will be in the interest of the patient to leave them undisturbed, except and unless there is demonstrable evidence that they are doing harm.

The intra-abdominal injection of oxygen and nitrous oxide in conjunction with radiography, a recent addition in abdominal diagnosis, is likely to become a valuable adjunct in the diagnosis of adhesions and other obscure pathological intra-abdominal conditions-Chronic pancreatitis, per se, is a comparatively uncommon disease in most countries. In India the disease has not been frequently diagnosed. Lack of definiteness, or at least positiveness, in the symptomology accounts in part for the failure of recognition. The comparative infrequence of gall stones with which pancreatitis is commonly associated is a further reason for the dearth of reported cases. We have observed a good many cases with enlarged head of the pancreas in operations for duodenal ulcer with the ulcer adherent to the pancreas; the pancreatitis being probably secondary to the ulcer. Spasm and obstruction by intestinal worms including pylorospasm may give rise to symptoms resembling ulcer. It is a good rule in Inidiia not only to examine the stools in every prospective abdominal operation, excepting, of course, acute cases, and to prescribe an anthelmintic as a part of the preparation. We have in four instances operated for intestinal obstruction due to plugging of the bowel by masses of coiled-up Ascaris lumbricoides.

In a recent case of some months' duration, the symptoms resembled duodenal ulcer. Exploration revealed a large bunch of snarled worms impacted in the upper jejunum with a greatly thickened pylorus present, but no visible scar. The worms (40 in all) were removed through a small incision, and the Rammstedt operation mentioned above performed on the pylorus.

Epigastric hernia is a condition which may give rise to pain suggesting gastric trouble, and may easily be overlooked. Maschcowitz, of New York, has recently emphasized this fact in the report of cases. We have operated on three such in recent years.

That ulcer can be cured by diet and medication Sippy and others have conclusively shown. The treatment requires careful dieting, forced rest over a long period which the average Indian villager can neither afford nor secure. Furthermore, cases of medical cure may and do relapse. Most of these patients in this country seek surgical relief after what Dr. W. J. Mayo calls their " nine medical cures " and are eager for any form of treatment that promises speedy relief. Gastro-enterostomy is now a thoroughly established operation in duodenal ulcer, and the same operation, with or without excision of the ulcer, in gastric ulcer. In our experience, posterior gastro-enterostomy, when performed with proper indications, is one of the most satisfactory operations in the whole range of surgery. A description of the operation here would be superfluous. The no-loop operation with the efferent jejunal loop to the left and a two to two and-a-half inch stoma is our choice. We have found the operation sufficient in the majority of gastric as well as duodenal ulcers.

In but few cases have we resorted to excision of the stomach ulcer, and then only when the ulcer was easily accessible. Our reason for the disinclination to excise the ulcer in most cases is that the average Indian, in our experience, is a poorer surgical risk than the European and is more susceptible of post-operative pulmonary complications, especially in operations of the upper abdomen. With few exceptions, our mortality in gastro-enterostomy and operations in the upper abdomen has been the result of post-operative pneumonia.

The practice of some surgeons of excluding duodenal ulcer by ligation of the pylorus, I did Dec., 1920.] BLOOD PRESSURE & QUININE TREATMENT: BRAHMACHARI. 447 not find a common procedure in the various American clinics I had the opportunity of visiting on my furlough in 1917-18. In three cases we added ligation to gastro-enterostomy without appreciable result one way or the other. The value of gastro-enterostomy has been shown in a recent post-operative investigation by Bulfour. This consisted in a comparison of the mortality in a given number of persons of certain age and social status in ordinary life, during a six-year period, with a similar number of persons upon whom gastroenterostomy had been performed for gastric and duodenal ulcer. The result was, after the second year, actually in favour of those who had undergone operation for duodenal ulcer. The statistics were much less favourable in the gastric cases, the death-rate during three anid-a-half years was three-and-two-third times the deathrate of the general population. The observation demonstrates the greater seriousness of gastric ulcer as compared with duodenal ulcer, a fact due most probably to the development of cancer on the site of gastric ulcer and is in favour of excision of the ulcer. Cancer, as is well known, is rarely super-imposed upon a duodenal ulcer.
Unfortunately the comparison cited above is at present impossible of repetition in India owing to the unreliability of mortality statistics and the impracticability of a reliable fo'llow-up system.

Finally, I should like to add a word regarding needless gastro-enterostomies. I presume every surgeon of experience has 011 one or more occasions performed this operation without a clear indication as to its utility. A great many needless gastro-enterostomies have been performed, with the result that in not a few cases the patient's last condition was worse than the first. This was inevitable in the earlier days of inexperience in gastric surgery. Tonday, however, in the light of present knowledge of living pathology, there is no valid excuse for this admitted error of judgment of former days. The necessary criterion for the operation is the presence on exposure of a visible or palpable ulcer, the history of which is compatible with the operative findings.

enlarged pancreas in conjunction with duodenal ulcer are, in our experience, poor operative risks for gastro-enterostomy. Gall-bladder or gall duct drainage is more likely to be of service.Tumours of the pancreas.?Statistics given byOsier from three large European and one American Hospitals gave 183 cases of cancer of the pancreas in 37,641 autopsies, 1 in 209; sarcoma is exceedingly rare. Pancreatic cyst is not infrequent. We have histories of three cases, two of which were cured by simple drainage, attaching the cyst wall to the parietal peritoneum. Bismuth paste injection helped the final closing of the drainage tract. Early growth in the pancreas may require exploration in order to differentiate it from ulcer or gastric cancer.
